verses.text: Now these are the last words of David. David the son of Jesse says, the man who was raised on high says, the anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel:
“Yahweh’s Spirit spoke by me. His word was on my tongue.
The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me, ‘One who rules over men righteously, who rules in the fear of God,
shall be as the light of the morning, when the sun rises, a morning without clouds, when the tender grass springs out of the earth, through clear shining after rain.’

Most certainly my house is not so with God, yet he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things, and sure, for it is all my salvation, and all my desire, although he doesn’t make it grow.
But all the ungodly will be as thorns to be thrust away, because they can’t be taken with the hand,
But the man who touches them must be armed with iron and the staff of a spear. They will be utterly burned with fire in their place.”
These are the names of the mighty men whom David had: Josheb Basshebeth a Tahchemonite, chief of the captains; the same was Adino the Eznite, against eight hundred slain at one time.

After him was Eleazar the son of Dodai the son of an Ahohite, one of the three mighty men with David, when they defied the Philistines who were there gathered together to battle, and the men of Israel had gone away.
He arose and struck the Philistines until his hand was weary, and his hand froze to the sword; and Yahweh worked a great victory that day; and the people returned after him only to take plunder.
After him was Shammah the son of Agee a Hararite. The Philistines had gathered together into a troop, where there was a plot of ground full of lentils; and the people fled from the Philistines.
But he stood in the middle of the plot and defended it, and killed the Philistines; and Yahweh worked a great victory.
Three of the thirty chief men went down, and came to David in the harvest time to the cave of Adullam; and the troop of the Philistines was encamped in the valley of Rephaim.
David was then in the stronghold; and the garrison of the Philistines was then in Bethlehem.
David longed, and said, “Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem, which is by the gate!”

The three mighty men broke through the army of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate, and took it and brought it to David; but he would not drink of it, but poured it out to Yahweh.
He said, “Be it far from me, Yahweh, that I should do this! Isn’t this the blood of the men who risked their lives to go?” Therefore he would not drink it. The three mighty men did these things.
Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was chief of the three. He lifted up his spear against three hundred and killed them, and had a name among the three.
Wasn’t he most honorable of the three? therefore he was made their captain. However he wasn’t included as one of the three.

Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done mighty deeds, killed the two sons of Ariel of Moab. He also went down and killed a lion in the middle of a pit in a time of snow.
He killed a huge Egyptian, and the Egyptian had a spear in his hand; but he went down to him with a staff, and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand, and killed him with his own spear.
Benaiah the son of Jehoiada did these things, and had a name among the three mighty men.
He was more honorable than the thirty, but he didn’t attain to the three. David set him over his guard.
Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty: Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem,
Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite,
Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite,
Abiezer the Anathothite, Mebunnai the Hushathite,
Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite,
Heleb the son of Baanah the Netophathite, Ittai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the children of Benjamin,
Benaiah a Pirathonite, Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash.
Abialbon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite,
Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan,
Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Ararite,
Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maacathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite,
Hezro the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite,
Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite,
Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, armor bearers to Joab the son of Zeruiah,
Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,
and Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all.

footnotes.content: David's last words—he knows the end is near and speaks from a deep well. Listen to the weight of how he names himself: anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel. A whole life, spent—and what matters most is that the Lord's hand was upon him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh's Spirit spoke by me—David claims the prophetic gift, the very words on his tongue from God. This is the wellspring of his psalms, his prayers, the songs the people still sing in the temple. A man permeable to the Spirit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A king rules righteously not by strength of arm but by the fear of God—reverence, trembling before the Almighty. David learned this late and hard. True kingship is not conquest; it is obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Light breaking after rain, grass tender in the dawn—what a tender image for the reign of a righteous king. The world refreshed, the harvest brought forth gently. David draws from the creation itself to show what a heart turned toward God makes possible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: My house is not so with God—David is honest. His own sons will stumble, his reign will end in shadow. Yet the covenant stands, ordered and sure. Comfort is not in ourselves but in God's faithfulness to His word, not ours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ungodly are like thorns—fragile on the surface but dangerous. They prick the hand, they spread. The image warns: evil has no substance, no staying power, yet it injures all the same.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To handle thorns, you need iron and a spear. They are burned in their place. David is speaking judgment that belongs to the Lord alone—vengeance executed with fire. A sobering close to his prophetic words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Josheb Basshebeth slew eight hundred in one standing. A name that meant terror to the Philistines. These are not mere soldiers—they are the backbone of David's kingdom, the ones who bled to hold the throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eleazar held the line when Israel fled. One man against the Philistine ranks while his people ran. Faithfulness is not always flashy—sometimes it is standing firm when alone feels like the only truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His hand froze to the sword—exhaustion so complete that his fingers would not let go. And the Lord worked a great victory. Eleazar's faithfulness opened the door; God's power sealed the gate. One does not act without the other.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shammah stood alone in a field of lentils—not a high place or a fortress, but a plot of ground. The Philistines had come for the harvest, the year's provision. He held it. Sometimes faithfulness means holding the ordinary, the daily bread.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He stood in the middle and defended it. One man, surrounded, and Yahweh worked a great victory. There is no small place or small stand when the Lord is the strength. Every field is His, and He does not forget those who guard His own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three of the thirty came to David in the cave of Adullam during harvest—the cave where fugitives once hid from Saul (1 Samuel 22:1). Now these three seek David voluntarily, in his stronghold. The bond between a man and his faithful men is written across the land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David in the stronghold, the Philistines in Bethlehem—the village of his birth held by the enemy. A detail small on the surface but heavy with longing: a man cannot go home while it is occupied by those who do not belong.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David longed for water from the well of Bethlehem. Not luxury—water. The taste of home, a childhood familiarity. Sometimes what a warrior's heart craves is not conquest but the simplicity of where he began.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three men broke through the Philistine lines, drew the water, and brought it to David. An act of devotion beyond measure—they risked death for a cup of their king's nostalgia. David saw what it cost and would not drink.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Be it far from me that I should drink the blood of men who risked their lives. David pours the water out before the Lord—a libation, an offering of honor. His refusal is a gift back to the three: their sacrifice is seen, it matters, and he will not diminish it by drinking what cost them so dear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abishai the brother of Joab lifted his spear against three hundred and killed them. These men do not merely serve—they are engines of war, each one a fortress in himself. Yet even Abishai did not rank among the three greatest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Most honorable of the three, yet not included as one of the three—a curious distinction. Rank and honor do not always align with true greatness. The measure of a man is not always the measure the world sees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benaiah killed two sons of Ariel of Moab and a lion in a pit in a time of snow. One act guards the boundary against enemies; the other guards the flock against wild beasts. Both are the work of a man who stands between danger and the defenseless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A huge Egyptian with a spear in hand; Benaiah went down with a staff and took the Egyptian's spear from him. An image of faith meeting strength with grace—not matching force with force, but disarming through courage and quickness of wit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benaiah did these things and had a name among the three mighty men. His deeds are written down. Long after Benaiah is dust, his faithfulness is remembered in Israel's song. What we do for the Lord is never forgotten.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: More honorable than the thirty, yet not attaining the three—again, the pattern holds. David set Benaiah over his guard, the inner circle of protection. Honor and rank take different forms; a faithful man sees his true station and serves there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty. He died young in battle (2 Samuel 2:23), a loss that haunted Joab. These thirty are not abstractions—they are brothers, beloved, fallen and living, held in David's remembrance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite—names from the same clan. These men fought alongside kinsmen. Family bonds strengthened in the furnace of war become iron.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite—each name carries a place, a lineage. These are not cut loose men but rooted in Israel's soil. Their families know where they are called.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abiezer the Anathothite, Mebunnai the Hushathite—the list continues, each warrior named and known. To be named is to be counted, to be seen. David's roll of the mighty is also a roll of honor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite—places in Benjamin and Judah. These men are the shield of their own land, defending where they were born.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Heleb the son of Baanah the Netophathite, Ittai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the children of Benjamin—family names, tribal names, the texture of a people bound together by blood and oath.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benaiah a Pirathonite, Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash—men from specific places, their homes woven into their identity. When you know a man's birthplace, you know something of his soul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abialbon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite—more names, more places, each man a thread in the great cloth of Israel's strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan—generations marching forward, fathers and sons serving the same king, the same God, the same land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Ararite—names layered deep with history. These are not strangers to battle; their fathers knew the sword, and they carry it forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai the son of the Maacathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite—Eliam's father Ahithophel betrayed David (2 Samuel 15), yet the son stands faithful. Faithfulness is not inherited by way of perfection but chosen anew each day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hezro the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite—the roll marches on. Each name a testimony to a life given in service, a loyalty that has not wavered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite—men from the borderlands, from territories both in and beyond Israel's reach. David's circle reaches wide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, armor bearers to Joab—even foreign-born men stand in the ranks, trusted with the armor of the captains. A king who gathers faithful hearts regardless of birthplace builds a stronger throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite—two from the same small place, both named. The smallest corner of Israel is not forgotten when the roll of honor is called.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: And Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all. Readers today hear an echo in this name—Uriah, whom David took and betrayed, yet God restored to his people through repentance. Even shame, when laid at the foot of the throne, becomes a place where grace meets us. David's mighty men are not just warriors; they are witnesses to a king forgiven and held by God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
